This is why, when examining the impact on US manufacturing of external shocks, it is important to separate the manufacturing share of output from the manufacturing share of employment. 

When the manufacturing share of employment declines because of a rise in manufacturing productivity, this is a good thing, and is precisely the reason why countries should want to specialize in manufacturing. Even China, whose share of global manufacturing has surged in recent years, has seen a decline in the manufacturing share of employment. This is exactly the definition of productivity growth.

But when the manufacturing share of employment declines because of a decline in the manufacturing share of GDP, this is a very different thing. It means the country is reducing its ability to take advantage of rising productivity in manufacturing. This is clearly not a good thing.

I am always a little shocked when American economists dismiss the importance of manufacturing to the US economy by pointing to the long-term decline in the manufacturing share of employment in the US. This is not evidence that manufacturing doesn't matter. On the contrary, it is evidence that countries that specialize in manufacturing benefit from more rapid productivity growth.

Very interesting paper on the relationship between imports and household debt in the US. Note the conclusion: "We show that household debt increases significantly in regions in which manufacturing industries are more exposed to import competition."

American economists usually argue that it is the prior decision by American households to borrow and spend that causes the US to run a trade deficit. This study suggests causality may run in the other direction, so that those areas most affected by net imports are precisely where household debt is most likely to rise. 

Of course the accounting identity itself says either can be true.

FT: “China has rejected an EU request to voluntarily restrict its surging exports of hybrid cars to the bloc as the two sides enter last-ditch talks to avert a trade conflict.”

While this may be bad news for the EU auto industry, it doesn’t matter much to overall EU manufacturing sectors. Voluntary restraints can reduce China’s trade surplus in autos, but because they have no impact on China’s underlying imbalances, they can’t have much impact on China’s overall manufacturing surplus with the EU.

To the extent that voluntary restraints on Chinese auto exports to the EU would have benefitted EU auto producers, in other words, the benefits would have come at the expense of other EU manufacturers.

This does show, however, just how difficult it is for China to rebalance its economy and how dependent Chinese manufacturers are on foreign demand. Beijing has very little room to accommodate even relatively mild foreign needs.

US FCC to vote to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics https://t.co/hjV0mmTHyd

This is where a little understanding of why so much testing is done in China, in other words, understanding the market forces that lead to outcomes that should not be met with knee jerk reactions like "this should obviously be done in the US." Actual no. 

First, proximity to manufacturing. China remains the center of production for many categories of consumer electronics, including smartphones, computers, Wi-Fi equipment, connected devices, and telecommunications components. Manufacturers can conduct electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), radio-frequency, and other compliance testing close to factories, engineers, and product development teams. Moving prototypes between China and the United States for repeated certification testing would add cost and delay.

Second, the concentration of electronics design and engineering. China's Shenzhen–Dongguan–Guangzhou manufacturing ecosystem combines original design manufacturers (ODMs), contract manufacturers, component suppliers, product engineers, and testing laboratories. Many products from American, European, Taiwanese, and Japanese brands are designed or engineered in these ecosystems, even when the intellectual property belongs to overseas companies. This creates substantial demand for local testing.

Third, a mature international testing infrastructure. Testing in China does not necessarily mean that a Chinese company conducts the testing. International testing, inspection, and certification groups, including SGS, TÜV Rheinland, Intertek, and UL Solutions, have established operations in China. Consequently, a geographical exclusion could affect laboratories operated by foreign multinationals as well as Chinese companies.

The reaction to this is typical response without bothering to understand how global supply chains work and where manufacturing is actually done.
